subject: Town Planning & Urban Management
title: II. Historical Perspective of Urban Planning

segments.text: Historical settlements demonstrate that planning is not a modern invention — different civilizations organized streets, water systems, defence, markets, religious and civic spaces, and housing according to their available technologies and institutions. The syllabus’s explicit instruction for this unit: for each civilization or historical example, ask a consistent set of questions —
settlement pattern, street form, water/drainage, public buildings, land use, defence, and what specific planning lesson it illustrates
— rather than turning the unit into pure, disconnected historical memorization. Any precise archaeological claim should be grounded in established archaeological sources.
European planning history moves through several distinct forms, worth naming precisely:
Greek
planning often emphasized ordered civic space and structured street layouts in certain settlements;
Roman
planning developed extensive road networks, engineered infrastructure, and gridded colonial/military camp forms (a distinctly systematic, repeatable planning approach applied across a wide empire);
medieval
cities, by contrast, often grew more
organically
, without the same degree of centrally imposed geometric order; and
Renaissance and later
planning reintroduced formal geometry and monumental design axes, reflecting a deliberate revival of classical planning ideals. The recommended focus, per the syllabus, is on these underlying
planning ideas and resulting urban form
, rather than attempting to memorize an exhaustive list of individual European cities.
Ancient Egyptian settlement was strongly shaped by the Nile’s river geography, supporting agriculture, transport, and the growth of religious and administrative centres. The existence of
planned worker settlements

in certain documented contexts (built to house labourers for major state construction projects) demonstrates that deliberately organized, planned layouts existed alongside more organic settlement growth in this civilization — a useful point for illustrating that “planned” and “organic” settlement forms are not mutually exclusive even within a single ancient civilization.

Mesopotamian cities developed around river and canal systems, combined with temples, defensive walls, trade infrastructure, and administrative centres — illustrating a close, direct connection between water management capability and the resulting form of the city. Dense neighbourhood patterns alongside centralized religious and administrative structures show an early example of functional zoning driven by both practical (water access) and institutional (religious/administrative authority) factors together.

blocks.text: .5 Mohenjo-daro and Harappa (the Indus Valley Civilization)

segments.text: These mature Indus Civilization cities are particularly significant for their
organized street networks
, sophisticated
drainage systems
standardized construction practices
(suggesting some form of centralized building regulation or shared building convention), and
differentiated urban areas

(distinct zones for different functions or social groups) — genuinely notable planning achievements for their era. The syllabus’s explicit methodological caution: these archaeological features should be discussed based on the actual physical evidence,
without inventing unsupported claims about the exact political institutions
that produced them, since the specific governance system of the Indus Civilization remains genuinely uncertain in current scholarship (the Indus script itself remains undeciphered).
These sites are significant for understanding the longer-term
prehistoric and early-urban development
trajectory of the wider South Asian region, providing an earlier developmental stage than the mature Indus cities discussed above. The syllabus’s specific caution: these sites belong to
different time periods and scales
than Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, and should not be presented as though they were identical in urban scale or form — a frequently tested point of chronological and scalar precision.

Gandharan urban and religious centres were closely connected with regional trade routes and broader cultural exchange, reflecting the region’s position along significant historical trade and cultural corridors. As throughout this unit, site-specific claims about particular Gandharan settlements should be grounded in established archaeological and museum scholarship rather than broad, unsupported generalization.
Key takeaways for Unit II

items.text: Apply the same consistent question set (settlement pattern, street form, water/drainage, public buildings, land use, defence, planning lesson) to every historical example in this unit — this consistency, more than historical detail memorization, is the actual skill being tested.
Kot Diji/Mehrgarh and Mohenjo-daro/Harappa represent genuinely different periods and urban scales within the same broader regional prehistory — a frequently tested chronological precision point.

The Indus cities’ organized street networks and drainage are well-evidenced archaeologically; specific claims about their political institutions are not — a strong answer keeps this evidentiary distinction explicit.
